title: Federal jury convicts Brooklyn woman who trained with ISIS in Syria - Whatfinger News Quick Hits
text:
A New York federal jury has convicted Halima Salman of taking military training from ISIS in Syria, the first U.S. trial of a woman charged with joining the terror group, with a decade in prison on the line.
Halima Salman, a 27-year-old former Brooklyn resident and U.S. citizen, was found guilty of knowingly receiving military-type training from the Islamic State of Iraq and al-Sham after a trial that ended in New York. Prosecutors said she pledged loyalty to the group, trained with an all-female ISIS battalion, and was authorized to carry ammunition and an assault rifle.
The verdict closes a long arc that began when Salman left the United States as a teenager, entered ISIS-held territory, and later returned to face federal charges. Officials framed the case as a clear warning: Americans who seek out terrorist training will be found and held to account.
The Daily Caller reported that investigators recovered a certificate confirming she completed the training, photographs of Salman posing with an ISIS flag in the background, and cellphone footage of her brandishing an AK-47 rifle. That evidence undercut any claim that her time with the group was passive or accidental.
A Department of Justice spokesperson said she was convicted by a jury in a trial that ended the day before the agency’s announcement. FBI New York, working with the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Eastern District of New York, handled the investigation.
Teen trip to “Turkey” ended in ISIS territory
In 2017, as a teenager, Salman’s father told her they were visiting family in Turkey. Instead, they drove into Syria. Their vehicle was surrounded by masked gunmen. For months they lived in buildings controlled by ISIS.
In 2018 her father was killed in an airstrike. Before that, he married her to an ISIS fighter when she was 18. Prosecutors later said she did not stop there. She voluntarily took weapons training from an all-female ISIS military battalion and gained authorization to carry an assault rifle.
The New York Post reported she trained with the female-only Nusaybah Katiba battalion and that this was the first U.S. trial of a woman on charges of joining ISIS. She was arrested in 2024 at JFK Airport after repatriation from a detention camp and now faces up to 10 years in federal prison.
National-security cases keep stacking up. Federal prosecutors have also moved against other alleged terror-linked defendants, including an Afghan woman tied to an Election Day plot the Justice Department sought to remove through a rarely used court process.
Prosecutors said she pledged loyalty and sought the training
The Washington Examiner reported that prosecutors stated Salman received weapons training and pledged her loyalty to the terrorist organization. The conviction followed a two-week trial. Jury deliberations included initial disagreement before the panel returned its verdict.
Assistant Attorney General for National Security John A. Eisenberg put the stakes in blunt terms after the verdict.
“The atrocities committed by ISIS, including mass executions, sexual slavery, and the systematic terrorizing of civilian populations, represent some of the gravest crimes of our time.”
Eisenberg continued:
“There is simply no excuse for aligning with or receiving military training from an organization responsible for such suffering. Today’s verdict sends a clear message that those who support this death cult will be found and prosecuted.”
FBI New York’s top official struck the same note. Assistant Director in Charge James C. Barnacle said Salman knowingly sought the training and absorbed the group’s ideology.
“Halima Salman knowingly sought out terrorist training from ISIS in Syria, she subscribed to their belief system and learned how to use weapons of mass violence.”
Barnacle added that defending the homeland remains the FBI’s top priority and that anyone found guilty of supporting a foreign terrorist organization will be investigated and prosecuted. He called the verdict a victory in the fight against terrorism inside the United States.
Cases like this sit beside other betrayal-and-security files, from a DOE engineer charged in an alleged bid to arm Iran-backed Houthis to long-running fights over who gets to stay in the country after terror-linked conduct.
Arrest at JFK, historic trial, and a 10-year exposure
Fox News reported that Salman faces up to 10 years in prison, with sentencing set for Feb. 2. Prosecutors said she pledged loyalty to ISIS, married an ISIS fighter at 18, and completed training that authorized her to carry an assault rifle. A training certificate was recovered from her husband’s cellphone.
U.S. Attorney Joseph Nocella Jr. of the Eastern District of New York said the verdict holds her accountable for joining forces with a terrorist organization. He also said ISIS ravaged Syria and caused havoc across the globe, and that his office will continue to prosecute those who supported its murderous reign.
Breitbart reported she left the United States in 2016 at age 17 for ISIS-controlled Syria, married an ISIS fighter, completed the training as an 18-year-old, and was arrested in May 2024 at JFK after repatriation. She is believed to be the first American woman accused of joining ISIS to stand trial in U.S. federal court.
That first-of-its-kind status matters. For years, the public debate over ISIS “brides” and returnees often drifted into excuses, soft repatriation talk, or claims that young recruits were only victims. A federal jury heard the evidence, the certificate, the flag photos, the AK-47 footage, and rejected the idea that voluntary military training with a designated foreign terrorist organization is a gray area.
Accountability work does not stop at the courthouse door. Judges have also cleared paths to remove mosque leaders on national-security grounds, another reminder that the system can still put American safety first when officials press the case.
Evidence left little room for doubt
The government’s proof was concrete. Investigators recovered the training certificate. They recovered photographs of Salman with an ISIS flag behind her. They recovered footage of her brandishing an AK-47 on her husband’s phone. Officials said she voluntarily sought the weapons course with the all-female battalion and was cleared to carry ammo and a rifle.
FBI New York posted on the verdict the same day coverage moved nationwide, stating that after its investigation with the Eastern District, Salman was convicted of receiving military-type training from ISIS in Syria. The bureau again stressed homeland defense as its priority.
Open questions remain. The public record in this package does not spell out the full sentencing recommendation, the precise statutory counts beyond the military-training charge, or every detail of how she moved from a Syrian detention camp back onto a flight into New York. What it does show is a completed trial, a guilty verdict, and a maximum exposure of 10 years.
Vetting and returnee risks are not abstract. A watchdog review found errors in 40% of Afghan asylum cases from the Biden-era airlift, another data point in a longer pattern of weak screening meeting hard security reality.
Salman’s path, Brooklyn to Syria, marriage to an ISIS fighter, weapons training, arrest at JFK, and a federal conviction, is now a matter of court record. The jury did not buy ambiguity. Neither should anyone charged with protecting the public.
Americans who take up arms training with a death cult do not get a pass because they came home. They get a courtroom, a verdict, and the consequences that follow.
